grammar.title: Inverted Conditionals (Had I known, Should you need...)
grammar.explanation:
In formal English, we can drop *if* and swap the subject and the auxiliary: *If I had known* → **Had I known**.

This trick works with only three words: **should**, **were** and **had**. A true philomath of grammar learns all three patterns.

Use **Had I ...** for an unreal past: *Had I known, I would have helped.* (I did not know, so I did not help.)

Use **Should you ...** for a possible future, in formal style: **Should you need** help, call me. It means the same as *if you need help*.

Use **Were I ...** for an unreal present: **Were I** you, I'd accept the offer. Always **were**, never *was* — even for *I*.

Watch the classic mistakes: no contractions — **Had I not** known, never *Hadn't I known*. And never keep *if* — never *If had I known*. Many learners inculcate these errors by copying informal speech, so review the correct forms carefully.
examples: *If I **had known** about the traffic, I would have left earlier* → **Had I known** about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
*If you **need** help* → **Should you need** help, call me.
**Had I not** seen it, I wouldn't have believed it. (Never *Hadn't I ...*)
**Were it not for** your help, we would have failed. (Never *of*)
**Were I** in your position, I would accept the offer. (Always **were**, even for *I*)
